blocks.content: Design patterns are proven solutions to common design problems. Used well, they make your design elegant. Used to show off, they turn it into a confusing mess.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782974119698-982046788.png
The biggest mistake candidates make is treating patterns as the goal. They cram a Factory and an Observer into a parking lot just to prove they know them. Interviewers see straight through it.
This lesson teaches the mindset that actually impresses, then walks through the patterns you will use most, with code and clear signals for when each one fits.

blocks.title: The right attitude
blocks.content: Patterns are tools you reach for when the problem calls for them, and never before. Knowing when not to use one is as valuable as knowing the pattern itself.
1. Patterns Are Tools, Not Goals
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972235094-961036180.png
blocks.alt: Use a pattern only when it fits, otherwise plain classes

blocks.content: A pattern is worth using only when it solves a real problem in your design. The pattern is the answer to a need, not a decoration you add for points.
Do not go looking for a place to use a pattern. Solve the problem cleanly, and if a pattern naturally fits, use it.
The Three Families of Patterns
The classic patterns fall into three groups. Knowing the families helps you reach for the right kind.

{"headers":["Family","They deal with","Examples"],"rows":[["Creational","How objects are created","Factory, Singleton, Builder"],["Structural","How objects are composed","Adapter, Decorator, Facade"],["Behavioural","How objects interact","Strategy, Observer, State"]]}
You do not need all twenty three classic patterns for an interview. A handful, covered next, handle the vast majority of LLD problems.
2. Strategy
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972236590-98635748.png
blocks.alt: Strategy: interchangeable rules behind one interface

blocks.content: Use Strategy when you have several interchangeable ways to do one thing, and you want to swap between them cleanly.

blocks.title: Signal
blocks.content: When you hear "different types of pricing", "different payment methods", or "different sorting orders", Strategy is usually the fit.
Factory
Use a Factory when you need to create objects without hard coding the exact type at every call site. The factory decides which class to build.
Now the rest of your code asks the factory for a vehicle and never scatters new Car and new Truck everywhere. Adding a type means changing one place.
3. Singleton
Use a Singleton when exactly one shared instance is genuinely needed, like a single configuration or a single ID generator.

blocks.title: Use with care
blocks.content: Singletons are easy to overuse and can hide global state that makes testing hard. Reach for one only when a single shared instance is truly required.
Observer
Use Observer when many objects must react when one thing changes, without the source needing to know who is listening.
A freed parking spot can notify every display board at once, and you can add a new kind of listener without touching the spot.
4. Decorator
Use Decorator when you want to add optional features to an object at runtime, without a class explosion of every combination.
You stack decorators to build up features, so milk plus sugar plus cream is just wrapping, not fifty separate classes.
State
Use State when an object behaves differently depending on its current state, and you want to avoid a tangle of if statements.
Each state is its own class that knows how to move to the next one, which keeps the state logic clean and easy to extend.
5. Adapter
Use an Adapter when you need two incompatible interfaces to work together, wrapping one so it looks like the other.
Adapters are the glue between your clean design and messy external code you cannot change.
Signals That Suggest a Pattern
Certain phrases in a problem hint that a pattern might fit. Learn to hear them.

["Different types of pricing or payment suggests Strategy.","Notify all subscribers when something changes suggests Observer.","Create the right kind of object based on input suggests Factory.","Behaviour changes as the object moves through stages suggests State.","Add optional features on top of an object suggests Decorator."]
items: Different types of pricing or payment suggests Strategy.
Notify all subscribers when something changes suggests Observer.
Create the right kind of object based on input suggests Factory.
Behaviour changes as the object moves through stages suggests State.
Add optional features on top of an object suggests Decorator.

blocks.content: 6. Pattern or Plain Code?
Weigh the choice honestly. A pattern adds structure, but also adds indirection that a reader has to follow.

{"pros":["A real, repeating need for flexibility","Behaviour that clearly varies or changes","A design that must welcome new types often"],"cons":["A one off case that will never change","Only one implementation, with no others in sight","Adding a pattern purely to look clever"]}
7. Do Not Force a Pattern
If no pattern fits, use plain classes. Most of a good design is ordinary, well named classes, with a pattern only where it genuinely earns its place.
Saying "a plain class is enough here" when it truly is shows more maturity than forcing a clever pattern that adds no value.
8. A Worked Example: Choosing a Pattern
blocks.text: 8. A Worked Example: Choosing a Pattern

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972238130-821294217.png
blocks.alt: Signals in the problem point to the right pattern

blocks.content: Imagine a parking lot that must support several pricing rules now, and probably more later. Which pattern, if any?

blocks.title: The reasoning
blocks.text: Several interchangeable pricing rules, with more coming, is the exact signal for Strategy. So we make PricingStrategy an interface and each rule a class. If there were only ever one fixed price, we would use a plain method and no pattern at all.

blocks.content: Notice how the choice came from the problem, not from a wish to use a pattern. That is the whole mindset.
9. Patterns and Principles Together
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1782972239715-963540106.png
blocks.alt: A pattern is a principle made concrete

blocks.content: Patterns are often just principles made concrete. Strategy delivers Open Closed. Dependency Inversion is what lets you plug a strategy in. Good patterns and good principles reinforce each other.

blocks.title: The connection
blocks.content: When a pattern feels right, it is usually because it is helping you honour a principle, like adding new behaviour without editing old code.
10. Builder
Use a Builder when an object has many optional parts and a giant constructor would be unreadable. The builder assembles the object step by step.

Pizza pizza = new Pizza.Builder()
    .size("large")
    .addTopping("cheese")
    .addTopping("olives")
    .build();
Builders shine when there are many optional fields, turning a confusing constructor with ten arguments into a readable, self describing chain.
11. Facade
Use a Facade to hide a complex subsystem behind one simple entry point, so callers do not deal with all the moving parts.

codes.python:
class BookingFacade:
    def book(self, user, show, seat): ...

blocks.content: The facade gives clients a clean, small surface, while the messy details stay tucked away behind it.
12. Template Method
Use a Template Method when several flows share the same steps in the same order but differ in some of them. The parent fixes the skeleton, children fill in the gaps.

codes.python:
class DataParser(ABC):
    def run(self):            # the fixed skeleton
        self.read()
        self.parse()
        self.save()

    @abstractmethod
    def parse(self): ...

blocks.content: The overall sequence is written once in the parent, and each child only supplies the parts that differ.
13. A Second Example: Choosing Observer
Suppose a parking lot must update several display boards whenever a spot frees up. Which pattern fits?

blocks.title: The reasoning
blocks.text: Many objects, the boards, must react when one thing, the spot, changes, and the spot should not need to know about each board. That is the signal for Observer. If only one board existed and never changed, a direct call would be simpler.

blocks.content: Again the pattern came straight from the shape of the problem, not from a wish to use it.
14. Common Mistakes

{"pros":["Reach for a pattern when the problem calls for it","Know a handful of patterns deeply","Explain why a pattern fits","Fall back to plain classes freely"],"cons":["Forcing patterns to look clever","Memorising all patterns shallowly","Using a pattern with no reason","Avoiding plain code out of fear"]}
15. Common Questions
How many patterns do I need for LLD? - A handful covers most interviews: Strategy, Factory, Observer, Singleton, Decorator, State, and Adapter. Know these well rather than all of them shallowly.
What if no pattern fits? - Then use plain classes. Most of a good design is ordinary well named classes, with a pattern only where it earns its place.
Is it bad to mention a pattern I did not use? - No. Saying "I considered Observer here but a direct call is simpler" shows strong judgement.
How do I remember which pattern to use? - Learn the signal for each, like several interchangeable behaviours pointing to Strategy. Match the signal, not the name.
16. Key Takeaways

["Patterns are tools for real problems, never trophies.","They fall into creational, structural, and behavioural families.","Know a handful deeply: Strategy, Factory, Singleton, Observer, Decorator, State, Adapter.","Match the signal in the problem to the pattern that fits.","If no pattern fits, plain classes are always acceptable.","Good patterns are principles made concrete."]
items: Patterns are tools for real problems, never trophies.
They fall into creational, structural, and behavioural families.
Know a handful deeply: Strategy, Factory, Singleton, Observer, Decorator, State, Adapter.
Match the signal in the problem to the pattern that fits.
If no pattern fits, plain classes are always acceptable.
Good patterns are principles made concrete.

blocks.content: Patterns are the polish on a clean design, not the design itself. With principles and patterns handled, the next question is how to present your work: UML first or code first.
